newsitem.title: USA: IBM moves closer to networked home PC.
newsitem.headline: IBM moves closer to networked home PC.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp unveiled Thursday a line of personal computers that breaks ground in turning PCs into networked home appliances that fit conveniently in any room of the house.

IBM said it has redesigned its new Aptiva "S Series" so a user has easy access to key features -- the keyboard, floppy drive, compact disc player, and monitor -- while the PC's main box can be stowed away under a desk, or perhaps a closet.

"The Aptiva split system creates a better fit between consumers and their home computers by directly addressing their distinct usage, space and styling requirements," said Jose Garcia, general manager of IBM's consumer desktop unit.

Even as these "split system" machines mark a significant departure from the clunky, all-in-one, beige boxes that dominate corporate offices, the new home PC line nonetheless borrows an insight from corporate personal computer systems.

By separating the central processing unit from the essential user controls, IBM said it is paving the way for creating home computer networks similar in key respects to the local area networks that now dominate office PC systems.

The new Aptivas reflect IBM's vision of extending home computers by locating "access stations" in rooms throughout the house that serve a variety of specialized functions, in effect turning the home into a computer local area network.

These smaller computing units would be linked to a powerful server, or central processing machine, that could deliver entertainment or video games to the living room or housekeeping and business tools to the study.
A home's lighting, heating, telephone and Internet communications, security and even lawn sprinkler systems could be managed in this way, according to IBM officials.
Eventually such systems could act as a bridge from the home to cable, phone and utility companies.
"It's as close to a grand slam as IBM has ever hit in the consumer market," said PC industry analyst Richard Zwetchkenbaum of International Data Corp, a Framingham, Mass.-based market research firm.

But Emily Green, a Forrester Research analyst, said that while the machines offer several promising new features, their premium pricing -- complete systems start at around $3,000 -- are likely to keep them out of reach of first-time PC buyers.

She noted that the entry of Sony Corp and several other Japanese consumer electronic giants into the U.S. home PC market is behind the drive by IBM and other established PC makers to make the latest home PCs more consumer-oriented.

"Sony has everyone else scared that Sony might be able to make a leap from last year's round of gray boxes to something new," Green said. "Everyone is trying to show they can think out of the box -- literally out of the gray box."

IBM ranked behind Packard Bell Corp and Compaq Computer Corp, the number one and two suppliers of PCs to the U.S. consumer market, according to statistics compiled by market research firm Dataquest for the second quarter of 1996.
